directAnswer: Pope St. Leo III, a Roman cleric of modest background, reigned from 795 to 816. After surviving a violent attack in 799, he crowned Charlemagne emperor in St. Peter's on Christmas Day 800, an act that laid the groundwork for the medieval Western empire. He was added to the Roman Martyrology in 1673.

paras: Leo had served as a cardinal priest and in the papal household before his election the day after Adrian I's death. He lacked the aristocratic connections of his predecessor, and Adrian's relatives in the papal administration resented him. On April 25, 799, during a procession, a band led by the officials Paschalis and Campulus attacked Leo, tried to blind him and cut out his tongue, and shut him in a monastery.
Leo escaped and made his way to Charlemagne at Paderborn. The king had him escorted back to Rome while Frankish envoys looked into the charges his enemies were making against him.

Charlemagne came to Rome in late 800. In December, Leo publicly swore an oath of purgation affirming his innocence, and the accusers were condemned. Then, at Mass in St. Peter's on Christmas Day, Leo placed a crown on Charlemagne's head and the assembled Romans acclaimed him emperor.

The event revived the title of emperor in the West for the first time since the fifth century. Byzantium regarded it as a usurpation, and historians still debate how far Charlemagne expected or welcomed it. In the long run it set a precedent that Western emperors received their crown from the pope.

Frankish churches had begun singing the Nicene Creed with the phrase that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son (filioque). When a Frankish delegation raised the matter in 810, Leo accepted the doctrine but refused to add the word to the Creed as used in Rome. According to the Liber Pontificalis he had the Creed in its original form engraved on silver shields placed in St. Peter's.

Leo enriched Rome's churches with gifts recorded in detail by the Liber Pontificalis and built a great hall at the Lateran decorated with mosaics showing Christ commissioning the apostles and St. Peter honoring Leo and Charlemagne. A later copy of the mosaic can still be seen near the Lateran.

After Charlemagne died in 814, a new conspiracy arose and Leo had its leaders executed, a harsh response that drew criticism. He died on June 12, 816. He was included in the Roman Martyrology in 1673, and his feast is June 12.

keyFacts: Survived an assault by Roman officials on April 25, 799
Crowned Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day 800 in St. Peter's
Refused to add the filioque to the Creed in Rome while accepting the doctrine
Built the Lateran triclinium with its famous mosaics
Added to the Roman Martyrology in 1673; feast June 12

faqs.question: Why did Pope Leo III crown Charlemagne?
faqs.answer: Charlemagne was the most powerful ruler in the West and had restored Leo after his enemies attacked him. Crowning him emperor recognized that power and tied the new empire to the Roman Church.

faqs.question: What happened to Leo III in 799?
faqs.answer: Relatives of Adrian I attacked him during a procession, tried to mutilate him, and imprisoned him. He escaped to Charlemagne and returned to Rome under Frankish protection.

faqs.question: Did Leo III accept the filioque?
faqs.answer: He accepted the teaching that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son but declined to insert the word into the Creed used in Rome.
